To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the swimming behavior and escape response of the ciliate S. spiralis reduce its vulnerability to predation by the copepod A. clausis, while the tintinnid Metacylis sp., lacking an effective escape behavior, was more vulnerable to predation.

the escape response of the planktonic ciliate Strobilidum spiralis significantly reduces its risk of predation by the copepod Acartica clausi, while the tintinnid Metacylis sp., which lacks such an escape response, is much more susceptible to predation.

The swimming behavior of 2 similarly sized planktonic ciliate species differed in their escape ability from the copepod A. clausis and this difference could be explained by their different swimming trajectories.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the swimming behavior of planktonic ciliated protists affects their susceptibility to predations by copepods.
the question of how differences in the swimming behavior of prey affect predation rates and thus the flux of matter and energy through planktonic food chains.
the role of behavior in trophic interactions and how this affects the fluxes of organic matter through the pelagic food web.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the swimming behavior of the ciliates is a key element for the trophic interaction between copepoda and ciliates.
the escape response of S. spirails significantly reduces the predation risk.
the swimming behavior of S. sp. is more efficient in escaping predation by A. clausii, and that Metacylis sp., which is more susceptible to predation, is more abundant than Strobilidum sp. in nature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that the escape ability and behavior of the ciliates are important factors that determine their vulnerability to copepod predation.
the swimming behavior of ciliates can affect their susceptibility to copepod predation.

we show that the swimming behavior and escape response of ciliates are important determinants for the risk of predication and thereby also for the flux of matter and energy through the planktonic food web.
The main takeaway from our work is that
swimming behavior can be a major determinant of the susceptibility of ciliates to predation by copepods.
the escape ability of prey can be an important factor in determining their susceptibility to copepod predation.
the swimming behavior of prey is a crucial factor for predation rates in the plankton.
